1.60.m: Skanda said: / I also ask about the sanctity of the fruit of another tree; / for the benefit of all worlds, tell us, O Lord of the Universe!
The Lord said: / The myrobalan fruit is supremely purifying, celebrated throughout all the worlds; / by planting which, a man or woman is freed from the bond of birth.
It is purifying to Vāsudeva, delightful, and auspicious; / merely by eating it, one is freed from all stain.
In eating it there is long life; in drinking it, indeed, an accumulation of merit; / in bathing with it, the destruction of misfortune; one attains all sovereignty.
In whatever house, O Mahāsena, the myrobalan is ever present, / into that house ghosts, Daityas, and Rākṣasas do not go.
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara— / the myrobalan alone is sufficient for men when Hari's day has arrived.
Whoever performs a bath with myrobalan on the eleventh day of both fortnights, / all his sins go to destruction; he is glorified in the realm of Viṣṇu.
The myrobalan fruit should always be used, both in eating and in bathing, / regularly on the day of breaking the fast of Viṣṇu, and merely for bathing on Hari's day.
Restrained, at the breaking of the fast, through the touch of a single myrobalan, / but the man who, having eaten, would transgress the eleventh day in the bright or dark fortnight,
yet through a single fast performed, O six-faced one, / he is freed from the sin committed in seven births—of this there is no doubt.
He attains imperishable heaven and goes to union with Viṣṇu; / therefore, with every effort perform the observance of the myrobalan.
Whoever's hair is constantly washed with the juice of the myrobalan, / he never drinks a mother's breast again, O six-faced one.
From seeing, touching, or even uttering the name of the myrobalan, / Viṣṇu, granting boons, faces him, satisfied and beloved.
And wherever the myrobalan fruit is, there Keśava resides; / there Brahmā and stable Lakṣmī dwell; therefore, one should place it in the house.
Misfortune is destroyed where the myrobalan tree stands; / and all the gods, well-pleased, do not leave it for a moment, in joy.
Whoever offers an abundant food-offering with the fruit of the myrobalan— / Viṣṇu is pleased with him, not even by hundreds of other sacrifices [as much].
Having bathed with the juice of the myrobalan, whoever worships Mādhava / attains his desired fruit, whatever is in his heart.
Likewise, remembering [His] characteristics and worshipping [Him] with the fruit, / the best of men attains the fruit of a hundred thousand gold coins.
Whatever state belongs to the wise, O Skanda, to the sages practising yoga, / that state a man devoted to serving the myrobalan fully attains.
That state which is attained by resorting to sacred fords and by various vows / is reached by men through devoted service to the fruit of the myrobalan.
And the affection of all gods and goddesses and of our host / turns toward [him], bestowing boons at the bath and at the enjoyment of the myrobalan fruit.
Whatever evil planets there may be, and fierce Daityas and Rākṣasas— / they all shed their wickedness through devoted service to the fruit of the myrobalan.
In all sacrificial rites the āmalakī fruit is praised; / in the worship of every god, excluding Sunday, O son.
Therefore, dear child, on the day of the sun, and especially on the seventh lunar day, / one should always avoid myrobalan fruits from afar.
Whoever bathes with and also eats the myrobalan on a Sunday— / his lifespan, wealth, and wife, all are destroyed.
At the sun's transit, on Friday, on the sixth and certainly on the first lunar day, / on the ninth and on the new moon day, one should renounce the myrobalan from afar.
In whose nose, ear, mouth, or hair of the dead / a myrobalan fruit remains, he goes to Viṣṇu's abode.
By mere contact with the myrobalan, a deceased man goes to Acyuta's dwelling; / all his sins are destroyed, and he goes to heaven in a chariot.
The righteous man who, having smeared himself with myrobalan juice, performs his bath, / obtains at every step the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
By the mere sight of it, whichever creatures are most sinful, / and all evil, dreadful planets, flee away.
Long ago, O Skanda, an outcaste Pulkasa went to the forest to hunt; / having killed hosts of beasts and birds, he was overcome with thirst.
Afflicted by hunger, seeing an āmalakī tree ahead laden with swelling fruit, / he quickly climbed it and ate the excellent fruit.
Then, by fate, he fell from the treetop onto the earth; / pierced by severe pain, he then met his death.
Then all the hosts of ghosts, and likewise the hosts of spirits and goblins, / all who are Yama's servants, [arrived] joyfully to carry off the body.
Those mighty ones were unable to look upon the dead outcaste; / a dispute arose among them as they cried, "This one is mine!"
Yet they were unable to seize him or carry him away between them; / then, taking notice, they approached the assemblies of sages.
The ghosts said: / "Why is it, O steadfast sages, that we, and also Yama's servants, / are not able to behold this sinful outcaste?
Those who die struck down by steadfast [foes] when turning back from battle, / those cast down by bold deeds, the frightened, those tormented by lightning, fire, or wood;
mortals killed by lions or tigers, or by sharks or aquatic creatures; / ghosts situated on water or land, those thrown down from trees or mountains;
those slain by animals or birds, those who have died in prison or by poison; / those who died by suicide, and those devoid of śrāddha and other rites;
the deceitful who died in secret acts, haters of preceptors, brāhmaṇas, and kings; / heretics, tāntrikas, the cruel, poisoners, and false witnesses;
eaters of food during impurity—these are certainly the enjoyment of ghosts. / Saying 'This one is mine!', yet we are not able to carry him off!
He is difficult to gaze upon like the sun. Why is this, or by whose power?" / The sages said: "O ghosts, ripe āmalakī fruits were eaten by him;
and copious fruits of that very [tree] came into contact with him; / by that very reason he is surely difficult for you to look upon.
When he had fallen from the treetop, the breath of life would not depart because of [the fruit's] affection; / he was not subject to the sun's course, nor [behaved like] other evil-doers.
By mere eating of the myrobalan, cleansed of sin, he will go to heaven." / The ghosts said: "We ask you indeed out of ignorance; we are nowhere revilers.
Before a celestial chariot arrives here from Viṣṇu's world, / let what is in your minds be told quickly, O tigers among sages!
Until the sound of twice-born [chants] fashioned from Vedic mantras and the like, / where the Vedas and diverse mantras are recited,
[and] where Purāṇas and Smṛtis [are read], we cannot stay for even a moment; / before the places of sacrifice, oblation, silent recitation, and acts of worshipping deities,
we do not stand at all; therefore let the account be fully spoken. / Having done what, indeed, do men obtain the womb of a ghost, O twice-born?
We wish to hear properly: how indeed does the body become deformed?" / The twice-born said: "Afflicted by the torments of cold, wind, and heat, by extreme hunger and thirst,
and by other sufferings—false witnesses, / and those who die by slaughter or bondage, have gone to hell as ghosts.
And those intent on finding faults, who ruin the rites of twice-born men, / and likewise those of preceptors—they become ghosts, without rebirth.
When a gift is being given to an eminent twice-born, whoever reviles the giver, / having resorted to the state of a ghost for a long time, does not turn back from hell.
Those fools who, having made a cow of another or of oneself into a beast of burden, / do not protect it, become ghosts on earth born of their deeds.
Those men who break promises, are untruthful, and have broken their vows, / and who eat on lotus leaves, become ghosts on earth born of their deeds.
Those who sell a pure daughter, a chaste and faultless wife, / or [property of] a paternal or maternal uncle and the like, become ghosts on earth born of their deeds.
These and many others have become ghosts by their own deeds." / The ghosts said: "By what action do men not become ghosts, O twice-born?
Speak quickly for our benefit what is the highest good of all the world." / The twice-born said: "By whichever wise man a bath has been taken in the water of a sacred ford,
and the supreme liṅga has been reverenced, that man is not born as a ghost. / Having fasted on the eleventh and especially on the twelfth lunar day,
and worshipped Hari, mortals indeed do not go to the state of a ghost. / And through hymns, mantras, and the like, born of the syllables of the Veda,
those devoted to the worship of the gods do not become ghosts. / Having heard the purāṇic discourse, divine and endowed with dharma,
and having recited it or caused it to be recited, one does not go to the state of a piśāca. / Purified by various vows and by wearing lotus-seed beads,
having chanted on a rosary of lotus seeds, one does not go to the state of a ghost at all. / Having bathed with the juices of myrobalan fruits, constantly devoted to eating them,
and having properly worshipped Viṣṇu with it, they do not go to the state of a piśāca." / The ghosts said: "From the sight of the virtuous comes merit, so the knowers of the Purāṇas understand.
Therefore your sight has been obtained; you ought to do what is beneficial for us, / so that liberation from the state of ghosts will belong to all of us.
O steadfast ones, we have approached you for refuge, [you who are] the instructors in vows." / Then all those compassionate, best of twice-born said to them:
"Quickly eat myrobalans for the sake of liberation!" / The ghosts said: / "O brāhmaṇas, at the sight of myrobalans we are not able to stand!"
How, then, can we now be capable of eating those fruits?" / The brahmins said: "By our word, the eating of dhātrī fruits here will be auspicious,
and it will bear fruit [leading] to the higher realm; therefore, you ought to go." / Then, having obtained the boon from them, having climbed the dhātrī tree,
the piśācas obtained the fruit and ate it playfully. / Then, from the dwelling of the gods, there swiftly [came] an auspicious chariot, large and very lovely.
Boarding it, the piśācas along with the cāṇḍāla / went to the third heaven, O son, which is very difficult to attain even by vows and sacrifices.
Skanda said: / Having obtained merit by merely eating dhātrī fruit, they went to heaven. / Why do men and others who eat it not go to heaven?
Īśvara said: / Previously, due to the loss of understanding, they did not know what was beneficial or harmful. / Leavings touched by dogs, phlegm, urine, or feces—
these the pretas, deluded, think to be the best, and eat them at all times; / and water for cleaning feces, vomit, offerings [eaten] by pigs and cocks;
and by whomever recitation of mantras is not abandoned during impurity from death or birth, / his food and water the pretas indeed eat at all times.
In a house where the housewife is untamable, lacking purity and self-restraint, / wicked, and expelled by elders—there indeed are pretas.
Those who are not prominent in family or caste, devoid of strength and enthusiasm, / deaf, emaciated, and wretched, are piśācas born of their deeds.
There is not a moment of auspiciousness for them; their bodies are afflicted with intense suffering; / for that very reason their forms are distorted, and they are devoid of all pleasures;
they are naked, afflicted with disease, dead, dry, and filthy. / These and others afflicted with misery belong perpetually to the race of pretas.
By such ripening of deeds they are born just as they wish. / And those who revile father, mother, teachers, and gods,
heretics, Kaulikas, and sinners—they are pretas born of deeds upon earth. / Those who kill themselves by a noose around the neck, by water, weapons, or poison,
in this world become pretas, taking birth among cāṇḍālas and the like; / outcasts, the fallen, and those who have died of sinful diseases,
and those killed in battle by outcasts—they surely become pretas upon the earth; / those tainted by the great sins, and those excluded from marriage,
and those who are rash out of false courage—they are pretas born of deeds upon the earth. / Those who commit treason against the king, and those who plot treason against their ancestors,
those devoid of meditation and study, and of vows, the worship of gods, and the like, / devoid of mantras and ablutions, and those devoted to having sex with the guru's wife,
and likewise those who associate with outcast women and wretched women, / those who die through cruel fasting, and those who die while dwelling in a mleccha land,
those possessing mleccha speech, though clean, and likewise those who depend on mlecchas for their livelihood, / those who follow mlecchas, those who subsist on women's wealth,
and those by whom women are not protected—they become pretas, there is no doubt of this. / When a brahmin whose body is tormented by hunger and exhausted has come to a house,
those who abandon such a guest of virtuous merit enter the state of piśācas. / And those who sell cows to mlecchas and cow-eaters,
after dwelling in the realm of pretas in comfort, they go to rebirth. / And those animals that are born and die within [the period of] impurity,
become pretas and piśācas for a long time, dying and being born again and again. / And those who are destitute of the rites of passage beginning with the birth ritual—
at each single rite of passage, the preta-state diminishes. / Sinners who have been destitute from birth of ablutions, twilight prayers, and worship of gods,
and of Vedic study, sacrifices, vows, and sacred syllables, become pretas without rebirth. / Those who throw vessels soiled with leavings of food and bodily impurities
into a sacred ford—they become pretas, there is no doubt of this. / Those by whom brahmins have not been satisfied upon the earth with gifts, honor, and veneration,
as well as ancestors and gurus—they severely become pretas born of their deeds. / And women who abandon a husband and dwell with other men,
after staying for a long time in the realm of pretas, are born into low wombs. / And those who deceive their husband, infatuated by the sense objects and the senses,
sinful women who eat sweet food [by themselves], become pretas upon the earth for a long time. / And those who eat feces and urine, those who are intent on consuming the property of brahmins,
and others who eat what is not to be eaten—they become pretas without rebirth. / Those who take the belongings of others by force and do not give,
and who disrespect guests, become pretas settled in hell. / Therefore, having eaten the āmalakī and bathed with its juice,
one is freed from all sin and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. / Therefore, with all effort, one should resort to the auspicious āmalakī.
Whoever constantly listens to this auspicious and sacred narrative, / his self purified of all sin, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
He should constantly recite it to people, especially among Vaiṣṇavas; / he attains complete union with Viṣṇu—so the knowers of the Purāṇas understand.
Skanda said: / The sacred fruit of the tree has been understood in its two kinds, O Lord. / Now I wish to hear of the leaf and flower that bestows supreme liberation.
Īśvara said: / Beyond all leaves and flowers, best of all is auspicious tulasī, / granter of all desires, pure, belonging to Viṣṇu, and very dear to Viṣṇu.
She is the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the foremost, supreme among all worlds, auspicious, / taking refuge in whom the best of sages have gone to the imperishable heaven.
For the welfare of all worlds, she was planted long ago by Viṣṇu; / the leaf and flower of tulasī are established in all dharma.
Just as Lakṣmī is dear to Viṣṇu, and just as I am dear [to him], / so is this goddess Tulasī; a fourth does not occur.
Even a single leaf of tulasī grants the fruit of a hundred golden coins; / neither by other flowers nor leaves, nor by other fragrant ointments
is Viṣṇu, slayer of the daityas, pleased without the leaves of tulasī. / By him who has daily worshipped Hari with this [tulasī] with supreme devotion,
by him gifts have been given, oblations offered, knowledge acquired, and sacrifices, vows, and the like performed. / Splendor, happiness, good fortune, fame, prosperity,
noble lineage, good conduct, a wife, a son, and likewise a daughter, / wealth, kingship, freedom from disease, knowledge, and discernment,
the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the scriptures, and the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Saṃhitās— / I consider all this held in the palm of the hand by the worship of Hari with tulasī.
Just as the Gaṅgā, of pure body, bestows liberation in the realm of the gods, / and just as the Bhāgīrathī is sacred, even so is auspicious tulasī.
What need of Gaṅgā water, what need of visiting Puṣkara? / One is delighted simply by water mixed with a leaf of tulasī.
He to whom Mādhava is favorable birth after birth, that wise man— / his faith arises, upon hearing this, to worship Hari with tulasī.
Whoever worships Viṣṇu with blossom-clusters and leaves of tulasī— / his fruit of merit, O Skanda, cannot be told at all.
The presence of Keśava is there where there is a grove of tulasī; / Brahmā and Kamalā are there together with the hosts of all the gods.
Therefore, one should always worship that goddess when she is near; / whether by hymns, mantras, or the like, all attains endlessness.
The pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, / bhūtas, daityas, and the rest who are there, flee at all times.
Misfortune, the destroyer, the dizzying [affliction], the ḍākinīs, and other [evil] mothers— / all shrink away upon seeing a leaf of tulasī.
Sins like the killing of a brahmin, diseases born of sins, / and whatever is done by an evil counselor—all indeed perish there.
By whoever a grove of tulasī is planted on earth for Hari's sake, / by him a hundred sacrifices have been performed according to the rules, with generous priestly gifts.
And in the symbols of Hari, and in others, and upon the śālagrāma stone, / having taken tulasī, one goes to union with Viṣṇu.
His ancestors rejoice; and whichever wise man plants / tulasī on the earth for Mādhava's sake, he goes to Mādhava's abode.
Having worshipped the god Hari, whoever bears the offered tulasī leaf / on his head, purified from sin, goes to heaven.
In worship, in praising, in meditation, in planting, and in wearing, in the Kali age, / tulasī burns away sin and bestows heaven and liberation.
Whoever gives instruction about her and also practices it himself,
he goes to the supreme station, the abode of Mādhava. / And whatever pleases Hari becomes even dearer to me,
and equal on all sides among all the gods and goddesses. / In ancestral rites and in sacrificial acts, a single leaf, O six-faced one!
Therefore, with every effort, serve tulasī. / By whoever tulasī has been served, by him indeed everything has been served.
Therefore serve the guru, the Brahmin, the deity, and the sacred ford, O six-faced one! / But whoever gives up his life-breaths having placed tulasī upon his crest-lock,
freed from a flood of wicked deeds, he goes to diseased-free heaven. / By sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, and by various vows and restraints,
the goal that is attained by the wise becomes the portion of those who serve tulasī. / And having worshipped Hari with a single tulasī leaf, a person
attains the state of a Vaiṣṇava; what use are other extensive scriptures? / He will not drink the milk of a mother! By crore-numbered
soft branch-sprouts of tulasī, by which Keśava is worshipped, / that mortal sanctifies ancestors by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Having worshipped Hari constantly with tender tulasī leaves, / the virtues of tulasī have been declared by me in main points, my dear.
We are not able to tell its complete virtues even in a long time. / But whoever hears constantly this narrative, which is an accumulation of merit,
he is freed from sin committed in previous births and from the bondage of birth. / By merely reciting it once, he obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Diseases do not come to him, nor foolishness ever to his son. / He always attains victory; he will not suffer defeat.
In whose house the written text stays, for him Fortune thrives. / Neither mental agonies, nor spirits, nor grief, nor humiliation
dwell even for a moment where this writing is present.

1.61.m: The twice-born said: / The auspicious glorification of the tulasī flower of Hari has been heard from you. / We wish to hear the meritorious hymn composed for her.
Vyāsa said: / What was proclaimed by me formerly in the Skanda Purāṇa, O twice-born, / that ancient account I relate before you for the sake of liberation.
The disciples of the sage Śatānanda, all of them of strict vows, / having bowed down to their guru, the Brahmins asked him for their welfare with respect to merit:
"Formerly heard from the mouth of Brahmā, O lord, that hymn to tulasī, / that we wish to hear from you, O best of knowers of Brahman!"
Śatānanda said: / When the utterance of her name is made, the destroyer of the pride of demons is pleased; / sins dissolve away, and merit becomes imperishable.
How should that tulasī not be worshipped and praised by the worlds, / through the sight of whom alone [the merit of] a gift of a crore of cows is obtained?
Blessed are those mortals in the world in whose house it is present in the Kali age! / For the sake of the śālagrāma stone, tulasī [is gathered] daily on earth;
blessed are those sprout-like hands of theirs who gather tulasī. / And those who plant it here on the earth for Keśava's sake in the Kali age,
what will even an enraged Yama do to them along with his servants? / By whom the lord of the gods, the remover of sorrow, is worshipped with a tulasī leaf,
with fruits such as journeys on pilgrimages to sacred fords, what does a man accomplish? / In bathing, in giving, likewise in meditation, in ingesting, and in the worship of Keśava,
tulasī burns away sin; and in praising and planting it in the Kali age. / "O tulasī, you are born of nectar! You are ever dear to Keśava!
I gather you for Keśava's sake; be a granter of boons, O auspicious one! / So that with parts born from your limbs I may constantly worship Hari,
do so, O pure-limbed one, destroyer of the impurity of the Kali age!" / Whoever, having gathered a tulasī leaf with this mantra, should perform
the worship of Vāsudeva, it becomes a hundred-thousand and crore-fold. / The best of gods sing your power, O queen of the gods;
the sages, the perfected beings, the Gandharvas, and in the netherworld the king of serpents himself. / The gods do not know your power, except for Keśava.
The measure of your virtues cannot be told even in hundreds of crores of kalpas. / Arisen from the joy of Kṛṣṇa during the churning of the ocean of milk,
tulasī was formerly placed on the head by Viṣṇu. / Having reached these limbs of Viṣṇu everywhere, O goddess,
purity was attained by you. To you, tulasī, I bow. / So that with leaves born of your limbs I may worship Hari,
render me obstacle-free, so that I may go to the supreme state! / Planted on the bank of the Gomatī, tended by Kṛṣṇa himself
for the welfare of the world, tulasī [was tended] for the benefit of the cowherd women. / Wandering in Vṛndāvana, she was served by Viṣṇu himself
for the growth of Gokula and for the destruction of Kaṃsa. / Formerly, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, on the bank of the Sarayū, by Rāma
you were planted for the slaying of the demons, O beloved of the world! / Planted for the increase of asceticism, to you, tulasī, I bow.
In separation from Vāsudeva, having meditated on you, the daughter of Janaka / in the midst of the Aśoka grove was reunited with her beloved.
Formerly, for Śaṅkara's sake, O goddess, you were in the Himālaya / planted by Pārvatī for the increase of asceticism; to you, tulasī, I bow.
By all the wives of the gods and by the Kinnaras in Nandana / you were served for the purpose of destroying bad dreams; homage be to you!
In Dharmāraṇya and at Gayā, served by the ancestors themselves, / holy tulasī has been served by one desiring the welfare of himself.
Planted by Rāmacandra, served by Lakṣmaṇa, / and tended with devotion by Sītā was tulasī in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Just as the Gaṅgā pervading the three worlds is praised in the scriptures, / even so is the goddess Tulasī seen in all moving and unmoving beings.
And dwelling on Ṛśyamūka, served by the monkey king [Sugrīva] / was tulasī for the destruction of Vālin and for the sake of union with Tārā.
Having bowed to the goddess Tulasī, the crossing of the ocean was performed; / having accomplished his purpose and rejoicing, Hanūmat returned.
Having taken tulasī, freed from sins, one departs; / or, O tiger among sages, it removes the slaying of a Brahmin.
Whoever bears upon his head water trickled from a tulasī leaf, / he obtains bathing in the Gaṅgā, which yields the fruit of ten cows.
Be gracious, O goddess, queen of the gods! Be gracious, O beloved of Hari! / O you arisen from the churning of the ocean of milk, O tulasī, I bow to you.
Whoever should recite this hymn to tulasī during the vigil on the twelfth lunar day at night, / Keśava forgives thirty-two offenses of his.
Whatever sin has been committed in youth, childhood, adolescence, or old age, / all that dissolves away from the recitation of the hymn to tulasī.
The lord of the gods comes to pleasure; satisfied, he gives fortune; / and he causes the destruction of enemies, and bestows happiness and knowledge.
By the mere name of Tulasī, the gods grant one's desire; / even to contemptible embodied beings, the Lord of Gods grants liberation.
Pleased with the hymn to Tulasī, she grants happiness and prosperity; / know that sin standing on the path of Yama is dispelled with ease.
In whichever house the hymn to Tulasī is found written down, / there is no misfortune; certainly that person attains good fortune.
All auspiciousness is his; there is no inauspiciousness whatsoever; / abundance is always his, with plentiful wealth and grain.
His devotion to Keśava is unwavering, and there is no separation from Vaiṣṇavas; / he lives freed from disease, and his mind never turns to adharma.
He who recites the hymn to Tulasī during the vigil on the night of the twelfth day [of the fortnight], / whatever fruit is gained by thousands of crores of holy bathing places, by lakhs of crores,
that fruit he fully obtains after reciting the hymn to Tulasī.

1.62.m: The twice-born said: / By bathing, all sin certainly goes to destruction, / as well as major sins and others. Tell us the instruction regarding that!
Purified from sin, one enjoys imperishable heaven in the celestial world like Śakra; / there would be no loss of divine birth—tell us the instruction!
Here, everything supreme is to be enjoyed; when dead, [one is] the best of gods in heaven. / And for those ruined by the sins of Kali, the stairway to heaven is declared.
Vyāsa said: / O Brahmins, for ordinary people considering their fate, / because from the sight of men and women, the Gaṅgā quickly removes sin;
and by the mere remembrance 'Gaṅgā,' a sin is destroyed; / by praise, grievous sins, and by sight, heavy guilt.
From bathing and drinking in the Jāhnavī, and likewise from offering libations to the ancestors, / multitudes of major sins go to destruction day by day.
Just as cotton or dry grass is burnt by fire in an instant, / so from the touch of Gaṅgā's water, the sin of men would burn in an instant.
Through bathing in the Gaṅgā, one attains imperishable heaven and Keśava; / one obtains fame, kingship, merit, heaven, and ultimately the supreme state.
He who offers a rice-ball in the Gaṅgā dedicated to the ancestors, / according to the rule and preceded by the spoken formula—hear the meritorious fruit of that:
With a single [ball of] food, he is worshipped in the abode of the gods for a thousand years; / know it to be double with sesame seeds, and likewise with pure fruit.
With cow-products according to rule, O Brahmins, there is no end to his heaven; / in this way, through the offering of a rice-ball, there would constantly be [the fruit of] a hundred sacrifices.
Those ancestors residing in hell are fortunate, [and] those mortal dwellers / endowed with wealth and sons, healthy, honored with happiness and respect.
Those gone to the netherworld, and those who are insects on the surface of the earth, / in immobile things, flocks of birds, and the like—those mortals [become] wealthy kings,
when by their sons, grandsons, clan-members, daughter's sons, / sons-in-law, sister's sons, friends, allies, and dear or not dear ones,
water and a rice-ball are offered accompanied by suitable requisites / in the waters of the Gaṅgā or on its banks; their heaven becomes imperishable.
And whatever ancestors born of the maternal clan stand higher than the rice-ball, / all mortals become happy, by hundreds and thousands.
Those beings situated in his heaven, those situated below, and those living in the middle, / constantly desire the good Gaṅgā: 'May they go to the river of the gods!'
The ancestors of him who goes alone to the Gaṅgā are purified; / this indeed is the great merit: he crosses over and also causes [others] to cross over.
The Four-faced One is not able to declare the entire virtue of the Gaṅgā; / therefore, O Brahmins, I shall declare here some small part of the virtue of the Bhāgīrathī.
Sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and whichever other best among gods, / having performed austerities on the bank of the Gaṅgā, became imperishable in the heavenly world.
With a divine body and a chariot moving at will, / all of them even today do not return, indeed dwelling in mansions full of jewels,
where there are golden palaces, auspicious, going above all worlds, / fully filled with desired objects, where there are delightful women,
and flowering trees equal to the Pārijāta, resembling wishing-trees. / Having performed austerities on the bank of the Gaṅgā, they indeed attain sovereignty there.
Whatever state is achieved through many austerities, sacrifices, various vows, / and abundant gifts—that state belongs to those who attend upon the Gaṅgā.
An adulterer, a fallen man, a villain, an outcaste, a slayer of a guru, / one united with all malice, one accompanied by all sins—
sons abandon such a father, wives abandon their beloved, groups of friends / and all other relatives abandon him, but the Gaṅgā does not abandon him.
Just as a mother herself cleanses the impurity and dirt of birth, / taking them to her bosom, so the Gaṅgā washes away their impurity.
They become very famous, honored with enjoyments and ornaments. / When the Gaṅgā is viewed even once with devotion by men,
the auspicious river delivers a hundred thousand of their families from worldly existence. / She who removes distress when remembered, by those who contemplate her, praise her, and are well pleased,
the Gaṅgā delivers both their lineages from the ocean of worldly existence. / At solar transits, at the Vyatīpāta yoga, and during eclipses of the moon and sun,
having bathed on an auspicious occasion in the Gaṅgā, one delivers a crore of family members. / Mortals in the bright fortnight, during the day, in the northern course of the sun, at the Gaṅgā,
are fortunate if they cast off their body with Janārdana situated in their heart. / He who, according to this rule, in the auspicious water of the Bhāgīrathī,
departs to heaven having abandoned his life-breaths, is free from returning again. / He who is always devoted to the Gaṅgā is indeed devoted to all gods,
since Viṣṇu is made of all the gods, and the Gaṅgā is identical with Viṣṇu. / By giving a rice-ball in the Gaṅgā, or with water and sesame seeds for the ancestors,
those in hell go to heaven, and those in heaven attain liberation. / Even for one intent on harming others' wives and others' property, and intent on malice,
as well as for an ordinary human, the Gaṅgā alone is the supreme goal. / For one devoid of the Vedas and treatises, and for one intent on reviling the guru,
and for one devoid of standard conduct, there is no refuge equal to the Gaṅgā. / What use are sacrifices rich in much wealth? What use are austerities very difficult to perform?
The Gaṅgā bestows heaven and liberation, worshipped with happiness and good fortune. / What use are supreme vows constantly? What use are yogic disciplines that restrain the mind?
The Gaṅgā bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, standing directly before happiness and liberation. / The accumulated sin of many births of men is destroyed;
by merely bathing in the Gaṅgā, a man instantly becomes a possessor of merit. / Whatever fruit one receives in Prabhāsa from the gift of a thousand cows when the sun is seized by Rāhu,
[one receives] from bathing in the Gaṅgā day by day. / Having seen it, she removes sin; having touched it, one obtains heaven.
Even when entered by chance, that Gaṅgā bestows liberation. / The fickleness of all the senses, arising from the power of latent impressions,
and pitilessness—these completely perish from the sight of the Gaṅgā. / Craving the property of others, desiring the wives of others,
and taste for another's dharma perishes from the mere sight [of her]. / Contentment with gain that comes by chance arises, and he engages in his own duties;
and equanimity toward all beings comes to be from immersion in the Gaṅgā. / The human being who, having taken refuge in the Gaṅgā, remains happily,
he alone is liberated while living in this world, the highest of all. / For him who remains having resorted to the Gaṅgā, there is no duty left to perform;
that human is one who has accomplished his task, indeed liberated, and liberated while living. / Sacrifice, gift, austerity, recitation, ancestral rite, and worship of the gods—
Whatever is done at the Gaṅgā, however, becomes millions of times multiplied every day; / and sin committed in another place is destroyed on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Sin committed on the bank of the Gaṅgā is destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā. / On the day associated with the Jāhnavī under one's own birth asterism,
a man, having bathed in the Gaṅgā, uplifts his own lineage. / Just as a man always praises a wealthy person with respect,
so by praising the Gaṅgā once, he becomes worthy of heaven. / Even without faith, whoever chants the names of the Gaṅgā,
of that river bearing merit, he indeed becomes worthy of heaven. / Sanctifying mortals on earth, and delivering the serpents below,
she delivers the gods in heaven; the Gaṅgā is recorded as flowing through the three paths. / Whether knowingly or unknowingly, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
a mortal who dies in the Gaṅgā attains heaven and liberation. / What state belongs to the wise man who is joined to yoga and fixed in goodness,
that state belongs to an embodied being who gives up his life-breaths in the Gaṅgā. / He who might perform thousands of cāndrāyaṇa fasts to purify his body,
and he who drinks Gaṅgā water at will—the latter is superior. / Only so long does the power of sacred places, and of the gods in particular, endure,
and only so long does the power of the Vedas endure, as one does not reach the Jāhnavī. / Thirty-five million sacred places—so Vāyu declared—
in heaven, on earth, and in the mid-air: they abide in you, O Jāhnavī! / O Gaṅgā, sprung from the lotus foot of Viṣṇu, moving along the three paths,
renowned as the liquid form of dharma: remove my sin, O Jāhnavī! / You are born from Viṣṇu's foot, of Viṣṇu's nature, worshipped by Viṣṇu;
protect me from that sin committed from birth up to death. / Filled with dharma through faith, and by your splendid sediment,
and by your nectar, O Great Goddess Bhāgīrathī, purify me! / Whoever bathes in the water of the Jāhnavī with these three best verses
is freed from sin committed in ten million births; there is no doubt here. / I shall declare the root mantra of the Jāhnavī, spoken by Hara,

1.62.s:
sakṛjjapānnaraḥpūtoviṣṇudehepratiṣṭhati
maṃtraścāyaṃ— namogaṃgāyaiviśvarūpiṇyai nārāyaṇyai namo namaḥ
1.62.d:
सकृज्जपान्नरःपूतोविष्णुदेहेप्रतिष्ठति
मंत्रश्चायं— नमोगंगायैविश्वरूपिण्यै नारायण्यै नमो नमः
1.62.m: from chanting which once a man, purified, is established in the body of Viṣṇu. / And this is the mantra: 'Homage to the Gaṅgā, whose form is the universe, to Nārāyaṇī, homage, homage!'
Whoever carries on his head the clay originating from the bank of the Jāhnavī, / that man is freed from all sins, even without bathing in the Gaṅgā.
If the wind shaken by the waves of the Gaṅgā's water touches him, / he is cleansed of terrible defilement and enjoys imperishable heaven.
As long as a man's bone rests in the water of the Gaṅgā, / for so many thousands of years is he glorified in the heavenly realm.
By casting the bones of one's parents, relatives, the destitute, or one's guru / into the Gaṅgā, a man does not fall from heaven.
Whoever carries a fragment of the ancestors' bones toward the Gaṅgā, / at every step that man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Blessed are the countryside folk, the beasts, birds, and insects, / and the other stationary and moving beings who have taken refuge on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Those who have died within a krośa of the Jāhnavī, O best of the twice-born, / are deities in human form; other men are merely mortals on earth.
If one sets out to bathe in the Gaṅgā and dies on the way, / he attains heaven and obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Those living beings that die on the way while journeying to the Gaṅgā water— / the insects, birds, and locusts crushed beneath the feet of those who are walking—
and the people, O twice-born, who speak of the journey toward the Gaṅgā, / those men also attain supreme merit, the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Those who revile the Jāhnavī, their minds destroyed by heretics, / go to a terrible hell from which return is difficult to attain.
Even a distressed person, constantly remembering and loudly proclaiming, 'Gaṅgā,' / and reciting her praise, attains heaven; what need of many words spoken on other matters?
Whoever says ‘Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,’ even from hundreds of leagues away, / is freed from all sins and goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
The blind and the lame who have not gone to the Gaṅgā / have their worldly origin in vain, meeting ruin as if by miscarriage.
Those who do not praise the Gaṅgā are the lowest of men, equal to inert matter; / they have not instructed others, being madmen of bewildered minds.
Those men who do not recite [it]—their sacred learning is completely fruitless; / they are evil-minded, fallen, and degraded, O brahmins, [deprived of] the fruit of the Gaṅgā's merit.
Those men who teach it and recite it with faith, / those wise ones go to heaven and deliver their ancestors and gurus.
Whoever gives provisions for the journey according to his financial means to those who are travelling, / and who travels relying on another's food, obtains bathing in the Bhāgīrathī.
One should know that the bath's fruit belongs to the agent, and double to the one who prompted it. / Whether willingly or unwillingly, by prompting or by service to another,

whoever has gone to the holy Jāhnavī would go to the abode of the gods.
The twice-born said:
The spotless praise of the Gaṅgā has been heard from you, O Vyāsa.

From where did the Gaṅgā come? What is her form? Whence is she so exceedingly purifying?
Vyāsa said:
Listen! Today I shall tell you the ancient and holy tale,
having heard which the best of men attains the path of liberation. / Formerly, having gone to the world of Brahmā, Nārada, the eminent sage,
bowed to the Creator, pure and sanctifying the three worlds, and asked: / 'What was created by you, O father, approved by Śaṃbhu and Kṛṣṇa,
and sought in the realm of the earth for the sake of the welfare of all worlds? / What goddess or deity is the highest of all,
approaching whom the gods, Daityas, humans, and serpents, / the egg-born, the sweat-born, the trees, and whatever other sprouting plants and the rest,

all attain what is auspicious, O Brahmā, and complete, eternal prosperity?'
Brahmā said:
In the past, by me as I was creating, Māyā in the form of Prakṛti was addressed:
'Become the primordial origin of the worlds; through you I shall create existence.' / Having heard this, that supreme goddess then became sevenfold:
Gāyatrī, Vāc, Svarlakṣmī granting all crops and wealth, / Jñānavidyā, the goddess Umā, the ascetic whose seed is śakti,
Varṇikā, and Dharmadravā: these are declared as the seven. / The Vedas originated from Gāyatrī; from the Veda the whole world is established.
Svasti, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Dīkṣā—these are recorded as born of Gāyatrī. / In a sacrifice one should always recite the Gāyatrī along with the phonemes and the rest.
In the sacrifice, having received the svadhā, the gods become ageless and immortal. / Thereupon the gods released the stream of nectar upon the surface of the earth.
Then the earth became possessed of crops, the supreme blessing of medicinal plants; / with fruits, roots, juices, and eatables, people became exceedingly prosperous.
Bhāratī abides in the mouth and in the mind of all beings; / in that very manner she provides instruction on dharma in all scriptures.
Higher knowledge, strife, grief, delusion and clarity, the auspicious and inauspicious: / without her the entire world lapses into non-reality; so it is traditionally remembered.
The lotus-born goddess is also the abundance of garments and ornaments, / and happiness and sovereignty in the three worlds; hence she is beloved of Hari.
By means of Umā, Śaṃbhu's knowledge is perpetual in the worlds; / she should be known as the mother of knowledge, dwelling in half of Śaṃbhu's body.
Varṇikā is the exceedingly fierce śakti that utterly bewilders all the worlds, / bringing about the preservation and destruction of the creatures in all worlds.
And by the goddess the two asuras Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain in ancient times; / and the terrible Ruru, renowned throughout all the worlds, was also slain.
She slew Mahiṣāsura, the sole conqueror of all the gods; / as mere sport the goddess struck down those asuras who were pre-eminent among Daityas.
Having thus constantly slain the forces of the Daityas, / this entire triple world was protected and gladdened by her.
She whose essential nature is fluid righteousness, who is established in all dharma— / having beheld that great one, she was held by me in my water-pot.
Born from the lotus foot of Viṣṇu, held upon his head by Śambhu, / and united with the three of us: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Celebrated as fluid righteousness, having the form of water in the water-pot, / she was produced in the sacrifices of Bali by Viṣṇu the almighty.
Formerly, Bali, the foremost of the mighty, was deceived by trickery; / then the entire surface of the earth was traversed with just two steps.
And the foot [reaching] heaven, having pierced the cosmic egg, stood before me; / that foot was worshipped by me indeed with water from my water-pot.
Having washed [it], the water fell from the worshipped foot onto Hemakūṭa; / reaching Śaṅkara from that peak, she wanders, settled in his matted hair.
Then, having propitiated Śiva, [she was] brought to the earth by Bhagīratha alone; / the foremost of elephants was continually propitiated with austerity.
By him, having cleft the mountain with prowess, an opening was made with three tusks; / from that [she is] Trisrotā, famous in the worlds, since she flows into three openings.
Purified through union with Hari, Brahmā, and Hara, she is the purifier of the world; / having approached that goddess, one obtains the fruit of all dharma.
Through all recitations and sacrifices, mantras, oblations, and worship of deities, / a creature does not attain that state which [is attained] through serving Gaṅgā.
For there is no means of accomplishing dharma higher than this; / therefore, through the merit of the three worlds, go to her, O Nārada!
And through contact of the bones with the water of Gaṅgā, those sons of Sagara / went to heaven together with their ancestors, both prior and subsequent.
Then, having heard [this] from the mouth of Brahmā, Nārada, the foremost of sages, / having performed austerity at Gaṅgādvāra, became equal to Brahmā.
Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, [yet] hard to reach at three places: / at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of Gaṅgā and the ocean.
In three nights or in one night, a man attains the supreme state; / therefore, with all effort, one should reflect on immediate liberation.
Therefore go, O knowers of dharma, to the auspicious Bhāgīrathī here; / within a short time you will attain heaven and liberation.
Especially in the Kali age, Gaṅgā grants liberation to men; / and an endless arising of merit [comes] to those whose strength is diminished by distress.
Then those brāhmaṇas, delighted having heard the auspicious word from Vyāsa, / performed austerity at Gaṅgā and then took the path of liberation.
Whatever mortal hears this unexcelled, holy narrative / crosses over the entire flood of suffering and obtains the fruit of bathing in Gaṅgā.
And when it is recited once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices: / giving, muttering, meditation, hymns of praise, mantras, and worship of the gods.
Whoever causes it to be performed right there obtains endless fruit; / therefore muttering, oblations, and the like should be performed right there by men.
Endless fruit has been declared, easily obtained birth after birth.

1.63.m: Pulastya said: / In this interval, previously, the great sage, the disciple of Vyāsa, / having bowed to his teacher, Bhīṣma's [charioteer] Saṃjaya, asks:
"Tell the definite procedure and order for worshipping the deities. / Who is to be worshipped foremost? Who is in the middle in daily worship?
And whose worship is at the end? Whose power belongs to whom? / Or what fruit does a man obtain, O holy one, having worshipped whom?"
Vyāsa said: / "One should worship Gaṇeśa first, for the sake of overcoming obstacles in this world; / he obtains the state of being a leader, just as he is indeed the son of Gaurī.
Pārvatī previously gave birth to two sons from Maheśvara: / Skanda and the Lord of the Gaṇas, heroic maintainers of all the worlds, gods.
Seeing them both, the mountain's daughter spoke for the sake of their accomplishment: / 'This sweetmeat, my sons, has been given by the gods filled with joy,
renowned as Great Intellect, fashioned out of nectar; / and I shall declare its quality; listen with attentive minds!
Merely by smelling it, one certainly obtains immortality; / he becomes a knower of the truth of the meaning of all treatises, skilled in all weapons and missiles,
proficient in all tantras, a writer, a wise painter, / a knower of the truth of knowledge and discrimination, omniscient—there is no doubt here.
Having attained superiority through dharma, my sons, he will reach a hundred accomplishments; / to him indeed I shall give it, and this is approved by your father.'
Having heard such words from his mother's mouth, Skanda, supremely skilled, / immediately went to all the holy places situated in the three worlds.
Having mounted his own peacock, his ablution was accomplished in a moment; / the wise pot-bellied one, having circumambulated his parents,
then stood before his parents, filled with joy; / and Skanda likewise stood before them, saying: 'Give it to me!'
Then, having seen them both, Pārvatī, astonished, said: / 'By ablutions at all the holy places, and by all the gods being bowed to,
by all sacrifices, vows, mantras, and by other yogas and restraints, / none of them equals a sixteenth part of the worship paid to parents.
Therefore, he is superior to a hundred sons, even by a hundredfold; / hence I give to Heramba the sweetmeat fashioned by the gods.'
For this very reason, worship belongs to him first in sacrifices, / and at the beginning of recitations of the Vedas and treatises, and in daily worship rituals.
The Lord of Creatures together with Pārvatī granted him a great boon: / 'By worshipping him first, may the gods be satisfied,
and of all goddesses, and of the ancestors completely; / and austerity becomes perpetual when the Lord of the Gaṇas is worshipped first.'
Therefore in all sacrifices, the twice-born should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas; / [the merit] of them is multiplied millions of times, according to the words of the god and goddess.
Having joyfully granted all virtues and merit, the god and goddess / then made him the leader of the gaṇas before all the deities.
Therefore, in abundant sacrifices, in hymns of praise, and in daily worship, / having worshipped Gaṇeśa, a man obtains all accomplishments.
Knowing thus, by the gods desiring to obtain their desires / and wishing for heaven and liberation, he was certainly worshipped by all.
Taking food at night on the fourth day, having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, / whether the god is worshipped in a liṅga, an image, or a painting,
[he should pray:] 'Homage to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, granter of pacification of all obstacles, / granter of joy to Umā, O wise one, protect me from the ocean of worldly existence!
Giver of joy to Hara, granter of meditation, knowledge, and discrimination, O Lord! / Homage to you, King of Obstacles, be gracious always!'
Whatever man, having fasted, joyfully worships the Lord of the Gaṇas, / freed from all sins, is honored in the world of the gods.
I shall declare his auspicious hymn of twelve names; / 'Om, homage to Gaṇapati' is pronounced as the mantra.
Gaṇapati, Vighnarāja, Lambatuṇḍa, Gajānana, / Dvaimātura, Heramba, Ekadanta, Gaṇādhipa,
Vināyaka, Cārukarṇa, Paśupāla, Bhavātmaja— / whoever recites these twelve names upon rising in the morning [attains success].

The universe becomes subject to him, and no obstacle will arise anywhere; / great spirits are pacified, and he is not afflicted by diseases; / freed from all sins, he indeed attains imperishable heaven.

1.64.m: Vyāsa said: / I will proclaim another hymn of praise to the lord of gaṇas, / which brings about all accomplishments, is pure, and bestows the fruit of all desired wishes:
"I bow to the leader of the gaṇas, who has a single tusk and a huge body, / who resembles molten gold, who has a pot-belly and wide eyes;
I bow to the leader of the gaṇas, who wears a muñja belt and a black antelope skin, / who has a serpent as a sacred thread, and has the crescent of the young moon on his crest;
the god who removes all obstacles, who is free from all obstacles, / who, having mounted the best of mice in the great battle between the gods and asuras,
is eager to fight, mighty-armed—I bow to the leader of the gaṇas; / who brings joy to Ambikā's heart, who is surrounded by the mothers;
who loves devotion, who is intoxicated with ichor—I bow to the leader of the gaṇas; / whose limbs are adorned with diverse gems, who has varied garlands as ornaments;
the god who assumes forms at will—I bow to the leader of the gaṇas; / elephant-faced, the best among the gods, adorned with beautiful ears;
the god who holds a noose and a goad—I bow to the leader of the gaṇas; / who is always praised by yakṣas, kinnaras, and gandharvas,
by siddhas and vidyādharas, having a huge body—I bow to the leader of the gaṇas." / Whatever man recites with devotion this auspicious eight-verse hymn to the gaṇas,
attains all accomplishments and is glorified in the world of Rudra; / likewise, that human being does not fall into destitution for seven births.

The man who recites this daily becomes a great king; / he brings the three worlds into subjection from reciting it, and even from hearing it; / this supreme, highly meritorious hymn of praise of the great-souled Gaṇapa [bestows this].

1.65.m: Vyāsa said: / Whoever worships the lord of gaṇas at all ceremonies facing prosperity, / everyone becomes subject to him, and his merit becomes imperishable.
With the mantra, "To the gaṇas...", and on vessels in all sacrifices, / a man attains all accomplishments and gains heaven and liberation.
In a clay vessel, on an image, in a painting, or on stone, / on the door-lintel or on a vessel, a wise man should draw Heramba;
and having established Heramba in any other place that is always within sight, / whatever wise man worships him according to his means,
his cherished tasks succeed completely; / no obstacle arises at all, and he brings the three worlds into subjection.
A seeker of learning attains learning originating from the Vedas and Śāstras, / and other mechanical arts, and victory which bestows heaven.
A seeker of wealth [attains] abundant wealth, a virtuous and delightful maiden, / sovereignty achieved through dharma, and a son who brings liberation to his lineage.
No one is afflicted by diseases, nor by planets, nor by ghostly states, / nor by horned animals, nor by rākṣasas, nor by lightnings, nor by forest thieves;
the king does not become angry, nor does a plague occur in the home; / there is neither famine nor weakness after worshiping Vināyaka.
Praise be to that lord of gaṇas, the destroyer of all obstacles, / who is worshiped even by the gods for the accomplishment of desired aims!
And this is the mantra: "Homage to Gaṇapati." / With flowers pleasing to Nārāyaṇa and with other fragrant ones, / with sweet modaka balls, fruits, and roots, and with offerings produced in season,
with curd, milk, pleasing instrumental music, and also fragrant incense, / whoever worships Gaṇapa attains all accomplishments.
In particular, whatever pleasing wealth, worship paraphernalia, or cloth / one offers to his liṅga, all of it becomes multiplied a hundred thousand fold.
And in the land of Bhāratavarṣa, in the presence of the eastern women, / on the southern bank of the Lauhitya river, Vināyaka is present in the form of a liṅga,
standing by the command of Hara and Gaurī and with the approval of the gods, / for the peace of the world, because he destroys all obstacles.
Having worshiped that god according to one's means with collections of articles, / a man becomes a leader and masters the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras.
Having made circumambulation even once, having seen and touched [him], / a human being attains imperishable heaven and is always worshiped by the gods.
For the higher destination of the mlecchas and companions, and of good ascetics, / and for the sake of sons for all people, Śambhu is there as Vināyaka.
Whoever, having performed a sacred bath in the Lauhitya, touches the lord of gaṇas, / is freed from sin committed in seven births—there is no doubt about this.
Having approached Vināyaka, one does not experience widowhood, / nor misery, nor sorrow, nor malice in birth after birth.
Accomplishment again, enjoyment again, fame again, and strength again / belong to a man after worshiping Gaṇapa—there is no doubt about this.
Without having performed his worship, every desired object is ruined; / there the gods headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are well-pleased.
Now, when Maghavan had abandoned the worship of Gaṇapa, / then, in battle with the very powerful asuras headed by Hiraṇyākṣa,
Maghavan was indeed defeated by Hiraṇyākṣa through his prowess; / then the gods were powerless formerly for as long as a hundred years.
In that great battle between the gods and asuras, there was the defeat of the gods; / then it was reported by the gods to Śiva, the god of gods:
"O Blessed One, our kingdom has been conquered by the asuras, and our sacrifices are gone!" / In the meantime, Śambhu spoke these words to the gods:
"A boon was granted to Heramba by me, being pleased: / 'Through worship of you, let there be supreme accomplishment for the gods and others.'
Whatever person through delusion disregards [him] at a great festival, / he shall have no accomplishment, and there will be defeat for him in battle.
In your great sacrifice, worship of Gaṇapati was not performed by you; / through heedlessness and delusion it was not performed; therefore defeat was incurred.
Go quickly to the meritorious [sanctuary] of the great-souled Gaṇapa; / perform worship, O knowers of dharma, and victory will soon be yours!"
Then, having heard the words from Hara's mouth, which were peaceful, supreme, and beneficial, / all the gods were overjoyed and stood before Gaṇapa.
The gods said: / "O lord of gaṇas, homage to you, the sole protector of all the gods! / O bestower of the enjoyments of heaven, with affection, O Heramba, we bow to you;
O giver of victory in all battles, giver of accomplishment in all actions, / having great illusion and a huge body, O Heramba, we bow to you;
single-tusked, of great wisdom, with a long trunk, Vināyaka, / the god of the great sages, of the gods, and of Indra—we bow [to you]!
Forgive us for that worship which was not performed formerly in our sacrifice!" / And having heard the words of the gods, Gaṇapa spoke these words:
"O gods, choose a boon from me that is desired by you!" / Then all [the gods] headed by Śakra, with Bṛhaspati at their forefront,
the gods said to Gaṇapati: "Let there be victory for us!" / Having heard the words of the gods, Gaṇeśa spoke these words:
"So be it, O best among the gods, let victory be yours quickly!" / Then all the hosts of gods, their minds filled with joy,
worshiped Gaṇeśa with essence of sandal and ornaments, / with celestial incense and fine garments, and with flowers born in the Nandana garden.
Worshipped by the gods with flowers of the pārijāta and other trees delightful to the gods, / the lord of the hosts spoke to the foremost deities:
"Go, O gods, to Lord Viṣṇu of wondrous valor; / he will fulfill your desire and your wish, O gods."
Mounting their respective chariots, they went to imperishable Hari; / bowing to the one clad in yellow, the hosts of gods spoke with joy:
"Having approached the son of Hara and worshipped the lord of the hosts, / we have now come before you today, O great-souled Keśava."
Having heard this speech of the gods, imperishable Hari / truthfully spoke this: "I shall slay the foremost Daityas."
Hearing the nectar-like speech falling from Nārāyaṇa's mouth, / delighted and filled with great joy, they worshipped him with choice offerings.
Again Viṣṇu spoke this to the gods led by Indra: / "Gathering your own forces, be ready and free from anxiety!
I shall destroy those evildoers and their army all around; / taking up your store of weapons, stand without fear!"
Hearing the word of Mādhava, the foremost gods set out, / having mounted their flying chariots, all bearing divine weapons.
The joyous words of the gods were heard by Daitya spies, / and they reported them to the mighty king Hiraṇyākṣa.
Hearing that, the king of the Daityas, who possessed great might, became exceedingly enraged; / summoning his ministers, he spoke in anger:
"Now Indra and all the other cruel-minded gods, / seeking to obtain Mādhava, reported everything to Śambhu:
'How shall we gain victory over the terrible multitude of Daityas?' / The enemy of Tripura spoke this: 'O immortals, worship Gaṇeśa!
Having worshipped that god, you shall conquer the Asuras and Dānavas.' / Then the leader of the hosts was worshipped by the delighted hosts of gods.
By the pleased lord of the hosts, a formidable and great boon was given: / 'Today you shall conquer all the Asuras.' Then the gods, filled with joy,
reported to Hari, seeking our destruction. / Hearing Hari's assent, chariot-warriors with weapons in hand
stand ready for battle, the immortals fearless toward me. / Let whoever has power here to conquer the gods speak out fully!"
Then, hearing the king's word, Madhu spoke these words: / "I shall conquer Hari, O king! Assign me assistance.
When Nārāyaṇa is conquered, the gods, the thirty [deities], will surely be terrified; / therefore Nārāyaṇa, the conqueror of all cities, is our share."
Then Dhundhu, Sunda, and the mighty Kālakeya [said]: / "We shall be assistants to that Madhu; O king, we shall conquer Mādhava."
The four chiefs in the entire Daitya army, possessing firm prowess, / heroes equal to Time and Death, master of the rules of all weapons [stood forth].
Bala then spoke these words: "The one in whom victory resides, / him and the victorious one [Indra] I shall conquer; this is my firm vow, O king!"
Namuci and Muci, the two brothers arrogant with might, / both spoke to the king: "By force we two shall conquer the powerful ones!"
Jambha also spoke these words: "Indra and those led by Indra / I shall conquer, there is no doubt; O Daityas, be free from anxiety!"
Tripura also spoke these words: "I shall conquer Vināyaka." / Then the general Maya, [and] the mighty Devāntaka said:
"Against Kubera [we shall fight] with the Rakṣases, and against all the sons of Hiraṇya." / In the meantime, the excellent sage Nārada,
having gone there, spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa: "I have come as the messenger of the victorious one [Indra]; / renounce the kingdom at our word, if you care for your life!
If not, fight with me today, or else go to the netherworld!" / Then out of anger he spoke this to Nārada, the best of sages:
"You are not to be killed today because you are a Brahmin; go swiftly from my presence! / Behold the calamity, slaughter, and death of the gods before [your eyes]!
Behold, O Brahmin, Hari, Hara, and the others brought to their end in an instant!" / Having spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas said to the commander of his army:
"Having made the army ready, bring all the chariots at once!" / Hearing the Daitya king's word, the commander of the army on all sides,
summoning the forces in haste, [saw that] they came swiftly, terrified: / thousands of crores and crores, and akṣauhiṇī armies.
And for each single warrior there were great mounts: / diverse chariots, as well as elephants, camels, horses, and donkeys.
Mounting lions, tigers, and wild buffaloes, they marched then, / with abundant instrumental sounds of every kind and terrible lion-roars.
They filled the quarters, the ocean shores, and the mountains; / and all the worlds were terrified, and the oceans trembled.
The drums of the gods sounded, struck by all the deities, / along with various other wind-blown instruments of deep, cloud-like sound.
All the worlds, terrified with fear, and whatever dwellers of the three worlds [there were], / their desires frustrated, looked to the sky at the terrible, fierce, great battle.
With iron clubs, nooses, spears, swords, staffs, and battle-axes, / and with sharp, terrible arrows, they struck one another in the battle.
With weapons and missiles discharged in many ways, all quarters without intermission, / in houses, upon the earth, upon mountains, and in the waters,
in temples, likewise in the sky, on mountain tops, on plateaus, / in caverns, and in the great wilderness, the battle between the two raged.
Like streams of water raining from the Puṣkala and other clouds, / weapons fell by hundreds and by thousands upon the armies.
Some fell to the earth, their bodies pierced by arrows; / others by spears, maces, iron bars, lances, and battle-axes.
The brave who fall facing [the foe], acting righteously in battles, / go to the abodes of the gods, being fearless on their master's behalf;
but those who are cowardly, wicked, slayers of those who turn away in battle, / and those who fight by unlawful means—they go to the abode of Yama.
The elephant-riders [struck] those standing on elephants, and others on horses struck those on horses; / chariot-riders [struck] chariot-riders, and foot-soldiers struck foot-soldiers.
The heroes, eager for battle, slew one another, / cheerful, full of courage, most righteous, surrounded by strength.
The mounts of some were cut down, their heads smashed by maces; / hairs, heads, and garments fell upon the surface of the earth.
Mighty warriors, cleft at the waist and severed, fell upon the ground, / and hacked and pierced by fierce strokes of swords and by battle-axes,
the steadfast warriors fell upon the earth, adorned with divine ornaments. / The region of the earth became ablaze with heroes, elephants, horses, and chariots,
with various broken ornaments, and with banners and standards; / then the entire earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves,
was flooded with torrents of blood there in the battle between the gods and the Asuras. / The mass of flesh was eaten there by many flesh-eaters;
copious blood was drunk by Rakṣases, wolves, and the like, / and the blood mixed with wind was consumed by other great hordes,
and with joy by glad packs of jackals and vultures. / In the meantime, the wise Bṛhaspati, worshipped by the gods,
chanted for the gods the lore that revives the dead, / the divine lore that removes arrows, the sacred wisdom of immense power.
Then the learned Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, swift as thought, / roamed joyfully in the battle with medicines and their applications.
There the gods who had died in the great battle revived; / free of wounds and endowed with strength, they fought fiercely once again.
Thus a hundred thousand of the arrogant host of the Daitya / fell, their necks pierced by arrows through the conjunction of merit.
Then, with shouts of victory, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, / ṛṣis, and other sky-wanderers, as well as hosts of apsarases, rejoiced.
The gandharvas sang songs, and the supreme ṛṣis offered praise. / Then, enraged, a mighty chief of the Daityas, possessing great splendor,
known as Kālakeya, the general of the Daitya king, / standing in his chariot, full of great valor, took up his bow there,
and struck those hosts of gods, making them reel upon the surface of the earth. / Then the sky was blanketed by a ceaseless flood of arrows.
Arrows fell upon the army in thousands of tens of millions; / then the gods, who never turned back in battles, began to fall.
All the Siddhas, gandharvas, and kinnaras vomited blood; / afflicted by arrows, the gods fell onto the surface of the earth.
Some were pierced by hundreds of arrows, others by thousands and tens of thousands; / those mighty bulls among the gods fell upon the earth in battle.
All the gods standing in their chariots were distressed; / sorely tormented by his arrows, they were unable to stand before him.
The army was plunged into by him as a grove in a lake is by an elephant; / afflicted by his arrows, which shone like the fire of a thunderbolt,
the gods could not hold their ground in battle and went then to Maghavan. / The god renowned as Citraratha, best among wielders of weapons,
mounted his chariot, took up his bow, and advanced toward the battle. / He too spoke these words to the great Asura general:
"Since you strike down the army of the gods with joy, O great hero, / you are praiseworthy, a hero respected even by the gods.
A deed pleasing to Hiraṇyākṣa has been performed by you in battle today; / now, through my arrows, go to the abode of Yama!"
Then Kālakeya, smiling, spoke these words: / "The entire host of gods was previously conquered by me with mere ease.
Now their whole force stands in battle only as child's play. / If you have a desire for death here, O bull among the gods,
with these sharp arrows I shall dispatch you to the abode of Yama!" / Having spoken thus, extremely enraged, [he shot] an arrow resembling Death.
The hero Citraratha struck it in battle, cutting it in the sky with three [arrows]; / again swiftly fitting arrows [to his bow] in battle in fury,
he struck many Daityas and cut them down with agility. / Then, with sharp arrows shining like the fire of cosmic dissolution,
the best of archers swiftly cut [his enemy's arrows] down to the earth in battle. / That battle between the god and the Daitya became exceedingly righteous.
Wishing to watch, ṛṣis, gods, and divine serpents came to their side. / Thus hundreds of thousands of arrows were checked,
and the two heroes shone in battle, each striving for victory against the other. / Then, enraged, the lord of the gandharvas, possessing great splendor,
pierced his forehead with three arrows and his chest with five; / he struck him with seven arrows in the belly, and with five in the navel and the bladder.
Brought down by the arrows, the Daitya was bewildered and fell into unconsciousness; / with his bow loosened, the mighty one regained consciousness after a long time.
He pierced the best of gods, known as Madhu, with three arrows; / and with his missiles he cut his bow before the eyes of the Daitya king.
Then, with thousands of arrows shining like the fire of universal destruction, / the mighty one, the best among the gods, pierced that lion of the Daityas.
His senses lost, with much blood flowing, / distressed and tormented by many arrows, that Dānava lord of the Daityas seized a spear.
While the spear was still in his hand, Citraratha killed his horses with four arrows / and brought them down, and with three [arrows] struck down his charioteer as well.
Standing on the ground, the Daitya then hurled the spear at the best of gandharvas; / the mighty Citraratha cut that spear to pieces with three arrows.
Seeing the spear destroyed like a serpent whose coils are crushed, / the mighty Asura took up a terrible club and rushed forward.
As that commander of the Daitya army approached with his club, / [Citraratha] swiftly severed his head from his body with a crescent-shaped arrow.
He fell upon the surface of the earth, and the earth shook; / then all the hosts of Daityas turned their backs and fled in all directions.

1.66.m: Vyāsa said: / Seeing his brother slain, the Dānava named Kāleya, / holding his bow and arrow, rushed toward Citraratha.
Seeing the Asura running forward, radiant as Time and Death itself, / the mighty Jayanta, the son of Indra, blocked him.
That best of the gods, full of great splendor, spoke to the Daiteya / words that were truthful, aligned with righteousness, and surely beneficial for both worlds:
"He who slays one tormented by pain from weapons, unconscious, encumbered by another, / routed, or disarmed is a fool.
After suffering in the Raurava hell for a very long time, he becomes that [fallen warrior's] servant for an age; / therefore, do not fight him; abide by the rules of battle!"
Stupefied with anger, Kāleya spoke these words to Jayanta: / "Having slain the slayer of my brother, I shall now kill you!"
Then Jayanta, the best among the gods, struck that chief of the Asuras, / who blazed like the fire of cosmic dissolution, with sharp arrows.
That Asura too cut down the arrows and pierced him with three [arrows]; / just as a river carrying red chalk swells upon meeting a downpour of rain,
so those two mighty warriors grew neither exhausted nor fainthearted; / seeking victory over each other, they found no rest.
Then Jayanta cut the Daitya's bow with an arrow, / and brought his charioteer down to the surface of the earth with five arrows.
With eight sharp arrows he brought down his four horses; / standing on the earth, the Daitya seized a spear and struck the prince.
Having brought down [Jayanta's chariot], battered by his mace along with its horses, / along with its fenders and chariot-pole, onto the ground, he let out a lion's roar.
With agility [Jayanta] jumped to the ground and stood with mace in hand; / just as the sound from a thunderbolt strike is unbearable to the worlds,
so did the clash of their maces resound again and again. / Thus their mace fight continued for four years.
When both maces were shattered, they stood on the ground bearing swords and shields; / then the duel of those two foot soldiers was wondrous and hair-raising.
Seeing it, the gods, Asuras, and great serpents were filled with amazement; / at the end of a moment, through the blows of their swords, their armors were shattered.
A sword fight ensued between the two skilled warriors; / Jayanta of terrible prowess seized him by the hair,
severed his head with his sword, and caused it to fall upon the surface of the earth; / then all the gods rejoiced with shouts of victory,
and the broken hosts of Daityas fled in all directions.

1.67.m: Vyāsa said: / Hearing this, the mighty king of the Daityas, Hiraṇyākṣa, / filled with rage and his eyes extremely crimson, gave orders to the Asuras.
"I am going myself to the battle, desiring to kill the gods. / If they do not come and do not fight, let them enter here from the path."
Having heard this speech, the remaining leaders of the Daitya host, / all of them very skilled with spears and nooses, marched out for battle.
With an army far greater than before, indeed a hundred times larger, / eager for battle, they marched continually through the sky.
Then the Rudras, with the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Vasus, / Skanda and Gaṇapati, led by Viṣṇu and Jiṣṇu,
all went out to fight, delighted and eager for war. / At that moment, a battle between the gods and the Dānavas [began],
such as had never been seen nor heard of before, striking terror into all the worlds, / filled manifold with weapons and missiles, like a forest in the cold season.
The battle flared up, encompassing the earth, heaven, and the sky; / they struck one another in the sky, and likewise one another on the earth's surface,
with javelins, pestles, broad arrows, and many showers of darts, / with cruel sword-strikes, and with discuses and battle-axes.
With various other weapons they struck each other down; / hideous forms and destructions appeared on the earth and in the sky,
with weapons, arrows, outpourings of blood, kites, crows, and jackals; / just as clouds pour down rain in torrential streams of blood,
even so the gods and Dānavas poured out blood falling from their own limbs; / some fell, some fainted, some stumbled, and some laughed;
they uttered cries of distress, and repeatedly raised lion-roars; / the arms of some were severed, and of others the legs were cut off;
some fell on the earth by the hundreds with their sides and bellies sliced open; / tens of millions of elephants, horses, and Asuras
fell upon the surface of the earth in many streams of blood upon the ground; / then indeed, on the surface of the earth, an ocean of blood arose.
Perverse rivers immediately flowed out in all directions; / the heaps of javelins and clubs were the grass and sticks in it;
mallets, pestles, and spears were its sea monsters and other beasts; / victory flags were the fish, and shields were the bodies of turtles;
they were dammed up everywhere by great piles of arrows and dead camels; / the flowing hairs and yak-tail fans were the moss, filled on every side.
And by various others falling into it, the sea of blood [spread]; / then the whole earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves,
became exceedingly terrible with torrents of blood, frightening all worlds. / By the fall of Skanda's spear, Daityas went to the abode of Yama;
by the supreme axe, by fire, and by arrows with tips of flame, / and bound by the noose of Varuṇa, they were submerged in the realm of Yama.
The sons, grandsons, vanguard, and ministers of these [Daityas] / were struck down by rains of arrows, javelins, and swords,
by the planets, by the winds, by Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, / and by the wise Kubera with his massive mace.
By hosts of clouds, thunderbolts, frost dispatched by the moon, / and the dreadful poisons of serpents, Daityas fell onto the surface of the earth.
Struck down by various other gods in hundreds and thousands of tens of millions, / all departed, their lives extinguished upon the earth.
Leaving their bodies, some went to heaven, some to the palace of Yama, / and some went to Pātāla according to their deeds of merit and demerit.
Meanwhile, the supreme sages muttered the Vedas: / "May there be welfare for the Brāhmaṇas, for the cows, for women, and among ascetics!"
While the other living beings were now fighting on, / the Daityas afflicted by the gods retreated to the mountains;
distressed and frightened in battle, they fled in all directions. / When the Daitya array was broken, the exceedingly powerful one named Bala
oppressed the gods, holding them in check with arrows equal to fire; / afflicted by his arrows, many gods proud of their strength
fell upon the surface of the earth, and some were broken on the field of battle. / Seeing his great deed, cruel and terrible to the worlds,
the sages praised him, while the remaining gods cried out in distress. / Then, enraged, Śatakratu, the tamer of foes, possessed of great splendor,
struck Bala, the foremost among the strong, with a dense mass of arrows. / Bala, too, enraged in the fight, hurriedly [struck] Śakra in return.
Both mighty warriors, their bodies soaked in streaming blood, / resembled two flowering kiṃśuka trees in the spring month of Mādhava.
The foremost of Asuras threw thousands of discuses, spears, / and pestles in the fight against Śakra, swift to strike.
The king of the gods, powerful and whirling swiftly in the battle, / cut down those discuses and spears with ease using his excellent arrows.
Then that Daitya of great splendor, with his spear, / swiftly struck Purandara, who was mounted on his elephant, right between the breasts.
Struck by it, Śakra reeled atop his elephant; / regaining consciousness, Jiṣṇu pierced the Danu-born Bala in an instant.
The slayer of heroes severed the hands and the bow of him who stood on his chariot with an arrow, / and cut through his sharp shield and standard with a single shaft.
With four sharp arrows he pierced the four horses, / and with a single arrow he cut off the charioteer's head at that very moment.
His bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his horses killed, and his charioteer slain, / he fell unconscious to the earth, and after a moment he met his death.
Then the great Daitya Namuci, the crusher of the pride of gods, enraged, / seized a mace and suddenly struck the great elephant.
Just as a thunderbolt would surely strike the peak of Mount Meru, / even so a great sound arose, causing the hair to stand on end.
Afflicted by the blow, the elephant reeled, bewildered; / its body drenched with blood, it turned away, racked with pain.
By hundreds and then thousands, [monsters] ran toward Śatakratu; / Pākaśāsana severed them with crescent-headed and razor-sharp arrows.
The foremost among the gods, oppressed by the creatures created by his illusions, / fell onto the earth, while some lay motionless upon their chariots.
Seeing his great deed, Mādhava, with his discus, cut down the arrows / that had turned into creatures and clung to the bodies [of the gods].
Then Jiṣṇu felled [Namuci] to the surface of the earth with three arrows; / having fallen to the earth, unconscious, the Daitya stumbled and rose again.
He grasped a dreadful mallet, prepared to slay Śakra; / then Maghavan struck the great Asura with his thunderbolt.
The exceedingly powerful one fell to the surface of the earth, his chest shattered. / "Well done, well done!" the gods, the Siddhas, and the great sages exclaimed,
