and they honored Śakra then with abundant showers of flowers. / Then all the hosts of Daityas fled in terror; / the Gandharvas sang songs, and the hosts of Apsarases danced.

Sixty-eighth chapter. / Vyāsa said: Seeing Bala slain, and Namuci his elder brother, / Muci spoke these words there: "My eldest brother has been slain by you!

Now, out of your sight, I shall send you to Yama with my arrows." / Śakra of great splendor, worshiped by all the gods, said to him:

"You will surely attain your brother's path of dharma right now, / just as moths, not knowing the heat of the fire, [rush in] out of delusion."

Just as [moths] enter fire precipitously, so you wish to fight me.” / While he was speaking thus, he struck Indra with three arrows.

Śakra, the conqueror of enemy cities, cut [them] off with three arrows. / Then he struck Indra with ten and Airāvaṇa with three.

Having struck Mātali with seven, he roared aloud with shouts. / In violent agitation the Daitya again whirled at Śakra

that iron club in fury, [being] of great strength and valor. / But then Śakra, with dexterity, struck [him] with the thunderbolt.

By the impact of the thunderbolt, he fell down lifeless. / By the fall of the Danuja, the earth shook.

The gods danced, and the Dānavas fled in all directions.

1.69.m: Vyāsa said: / Tāreya, endowed with strength and equal in valor to Śakra, / struck Skanda, the slayer of his father, with arrows in battle.
Then the mighty-armed Skanda, whose valor was equal to Hari's, / cut to pieces those arrows and pierced [him] through with excellent shafts.
Suddenly that Daitya covered Skanda with arrows; / unflustered, Viśākha then cut them down with his shafts.
Tāreya struck Skanda with fiery arrows at the head of the battle; / he drove an arrow resembling a thunderbolt into Hara's son.
There the commander of the army warded it off with a fire-weapon. / Then the Daitya sent against him the terrible Rudra-weapon.
That was warded off by him with a shot arrow. / The Daitya hurled the Aghora [weapon], terrifying in appearance and very dreadful.
Mountains, tree-branches, lions, and serpents in the form of arrows / rushed by tens of millions upon Pārvatī's son.
Having cut down those arrows, Skanda pierced the foremost Daitya / from foot to head with arrows resembling fire and the sun.
The gold-feathered arrows struck deep into the body of the Daitya lord; / they gleamed like flakes of gold upon a black mountain.
Then copiously flowed blood from his body, / just like an abundantly flowering Śamī tree in the month of Mādhava.
The horses running under his chariot lay clinging to the ground. / Then the enraged great Daitya, seizing a dreadful and fierce trident
blazing like death and time, hurled it against him. / With the Pāśupata [weapon], Pārvatī's son
consumed the hurled trident in an instant on the battlefield. / Then the Dānava again loosed a spear bestowed by Brahmā.
He struck back against the spear [with another] blazing like a hundred peaks. / Then both weapons, resembling thunderbolts, collided in the sky.
Both those mighty weapons fell down upon the earth. / Then the Daitya lord swiftly tormented Skanda
with arrows resembling crests of flame, as dense showers [strike] a mountain. / Having cut them down, the mighty-armed commander of the army
severed his bow with a crescent-shaped arrow, and likewise the charioteer's large head; / and he brought the horses down to the ground with many shafts.
Seizing a club, he swiftly ran on foot toward Guha; / with it the lord of Daityas struck the peacock and the rider of the peacock.
Then the peacock was stunned and trembled again and again. / Thereupon Skanda again struck that bull among Asuras,
and with his sword he swiftly cleaved the exceedingly terrible club. / Taking up a spear, Tāreya struck the piercer of Krauñca.
He too then loosed an unerring spear that slays the wicked. / Then, burning [his spear], that spear that brings about the dissolution of the universe,
resembling Yama's staff, pierced [him] and returned to Guha. / Lifeless, he fell to the ground, shaking the earth.
Skanda was worshiped with flowers, incense, and the like by all the gods.

1.70.m: Vyāsa said: / Then the Daitya Devāntaka roared toward the battle; / the powerful one fought Dharma, biting his lip.
Having approached, he spoke words condemned by the whole world: / “You do not know the highest dharma properly, out of wicked delusion.
[You are] master over punishment and reward through the application of sin and merit, / and I was created by the Creator; I carry out your command.
Because you do not know dharma, [you are] accompanied by time and death. / Neither disease nor old age, neither time nor death, nor any servant,
deviated from dharma, suffers misery day and night like an agent [of actions].” / Having spoken thus to the mighty Vasu, Yama, the sole witness of dharma,
he struck him with three arrows blazing like time and death. / The righteous one, however, cut them down with three other arrows.
Then with copious, towering shafts blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, / he struck Yama in the fight; and [Yama] cut down the arrows with his own arrows.
Meanwhile, the two enraged warriors, wishing to conquer each other, / fought one another in battle, both possessing great strength and valor.
Their exceedingly fierce battle continued day and night. / In the meantime, the tiger of Daityas, mighty and proud,
in rage pierced the Restrainer with a spear. / Then Dharma, seizing that very spear swiftly in wrath,
struck him violently with it between the breasts. / With all his limbs distressed, blood came from his mouth.
Then the greatly resplendent one, enraged, took up his exceedingly dreadful, / unerring staff, and brought it down upon that Daitya's body.
Together with horses, chariot, charioteer, warrior, and pile of weapons, / the Restrainer, overpowered by rage, reduced him to ashes.
When the Daitya had fallen, the Dānava named Durdharṣa, / trident in hand, ran toward the Restrainer, intending to kill him.
As he approached, trident in hand, resembling the submarine fire, / Death, utterly fearless with spear in hand, confronted him in battle.
Seeing Death, the Asura struck him with the trident; / and Death then hurled a spear upon the battlefield.
Instantly burning the trident that blazed like a mass of fire, / it pierced the Daitya's heart and went into the earth.
Along with his chariot he fell to the earth, his body shattered by the spear. / Then another of great strength, Durmukha, drew his bow against Death;
bearing sword and shield, Time stood upon his very chariot. / Seeing him, he struck Yama in battle with copious shafts.
The god, leaping down from the chariot, with his sword / severed his head with its earrings at once, casting it to the earth.
The rest of the army that was not slain fled in the ten directions.

1.71.m: Vyāsa said: / Then another [demon], Namuci, enraged, standing upon his chariot, / tormented the sky-dwellers with terrible shafts resembling venomous snakes.
Then in the clash the gods, Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas / were unable to bear the force of the arrows all around.
Mounting the chariot yoked with the horse Uccaiḥśravas and driven by Mātali, / Puruhūta went against that intoxicated [demon] of great might.
Seeing Śakra of great valor, Namuci, the foremost of Daityas, / then spoke words to Vāsava along with his followers in battle:
"By killing an ordinary god there is neither fame nor satisfaction; / nor is there any real gain, nor victory praised before all.
Therefore, if you alone are killed, everything becomes permanent: / I shall attain the sovereignty of the gods, happiness to be enjoyed in the abode of the gods."
Śakra, possessed of great splendor and conqueror of enemy citadels, said to him: / "Heroism would be easily obtained everywhere by mere words.
Whatever great valor you possess, lowest of Dānavas, / show your prowess in battle; I will send you to the city of the son of Bhāskara [Yama]!"
Hearing this, that foremost of Daityas of great splendor became enraged; / he struck the best of gods with five sharpened arrows.
Maghavan quickly severed them with five razor-sharp arrows. / Those two of great valor, desiring victory, advanced in battle.
They instantly cut through each other's arrows with arrows of great velocity; / then they pierced each other's limbs with shafts resembling thunderbolts.
An unprecedented feat indeed was performed by both of them in battle, / a swiftness in aiming, grasping, and discharging arrows that is extremely rare.
Seeing that, the hosts of gods and asuras were filled with wonder. / In the meantime, the Daitya released his magical illusions.
Hundreds of arrows flew out there in all directions. / The valorous Śakra then swiftly raised his bow again in anger,
and, blazing [with fury], struck [him] on all limbs with fierce shafts. / Then, with thousands of arrows and eight more in addition,
they pierced each other and severed each other's weapons. / The sky was seen completely covered with arrows in that battle,
and [heads and limbs] fell upon the surface of the earth by thousands from sword strokes. / In this way, when a very long time had passed in that great battle,
Namuci, who committed cruel deeds, then displayed an illusory weapon: / continuous darkness was created throughout the three worlds.
The hosts of gods and asuras could scarcely see one another. / Of the sun, the moon, the planets, the fires, and the dwellers of heaven,
in that impassable darkness, no beam of light could be seen at all. / And then, by the Daitya's arrows resembling flames of fire,
all the gods and Śakra were routed before the battle line; / pierced in their bodies by arrows, they fell upon the surface of the earth.
Other warriors were broken and fled in the ten directions. / Understanding his deception, Hari, worshipped by all the gods,
then released a gentle weapon in the sky, shining like a hundred suns. / Seeing [the demon] faltering, with a spear having many bells
he struck the Daitya in the chest; he fell, overcome with agony. / Regaining consciousness after a long time, the son of Diti was faint with rage.
Rushing with speed, he seized Airāvata, the foremost of gods' mounts; / in his fury, he greatly terrified Indra's elephant.
Having seized the elephant along with Indra, he cast it down onto the surface of the earth. / Then Śakra, fallen to the ground, lost consciousness for a moment.
Leaping down, that lord of Daityas stood between the elephant's tusks. / When he wished to seize Śakra to kill the leader of the host,
he [Śakra] severed the chief asura's head with a sword and struck him down. / All the gods rejoiced; the Gandharvas sang charming songs; / and the delighted sages praised the foremost of gods.

1.72.m: Vyāsa said: / Mounted on a celestial chariot, bow in hand, surrounded by forces, / having approached Mādhava in battle before the hosts of gods and asuras,
Madhu, the crusher of the gods, filled with great anger, / spoke harsh words to the imperishable lord Hari:
"O Nārāyaṇa, how is it that you do not know the dharma of combat? / Having devised an unjust means to kill me, are you not destroyed and grieving?
By this deceitful behavior of conduct contrary to propriety, / the godhood [of the gods] will be destroyed; I shall create another creation!
I shall kill you right here along with the hosts of gods!" / Having spoken thus and seized his bow, he struck the lord with arrows.
Mādhava then pierced them with arrows shining like thunderbolts; / and then he struck Madhu on all limbs with many [shafts].
Covered by illusion, that Daitya attacked him, O best of gods! / Whatever warriors there were—the Rudras and other gods endowed with strength,
various goddesses also, equipped with weapons and mounts, / generals, leaders of troops, gods, world-protectors, Hara, and the Viṣṇus,
and other gods such as the planets—all fought together. / And then those gods were indeed confounded by Madhu's illusion.
Facing forward and turning back, under rains of arrows, lances, and spears, / the gods, tormented by weapons, suddenly fell to the earth.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, taking up the Sudarśana [discus], / struck down the asuras who appeared as gods through illusion at the front of the battle.
Then, having severed their heads by thousands, / the lord of gods caused them to fall—[heads] of Daityas who had the form of gods.
In this way the lord put other Daityas to flight from the battle. / Seeing that, the sages and the gods were all filled with wonder.
The gods and hosts of sages whispered to one another in their ears: / "Hari, the imperishable lord, is always the sole protector of the gods;
this god is the witness of all, the conqueror of Daityas in every cosmic age. / How is it that he is killing all the gods? Is the end of the kalpa taking place here?"
In the meantime, at a distance, Madhu employed an illusion: / having assumed the form of Hara, he spoke to the imperishable Hari:
"O sinful one, having killed the gods everywhere in battle before the Daityas, / what good is there for you today, what virtue, fame, renown, and qualities?
Due to your great madness you do not distinguish between strangers and your own people. / Therefore, with sharpened arrows I will dispatch you to the abode of Yama!"
Having spoken thus, he struck Keśava with fierce arrows in the battle. / But Mādhava cut down those arrows and spoke these words:
"I recognize you in battle as the Daitya who has taken the beloved form of Hara, / the heroic Madhu of heroic deeds, who has engaged illusion.
I shall give you a false realm after striking you down on the battlefield!" / In the meantime, with sharp arrows he pierced in battle
the matted-haired, bull-bannered Maheśvara seated on a bull. / The battle between the two, the god and the Dānava, was then exceedingly fierce,
as they mutually shattered incoming arrows with arrows. / With a razor-sharp arrow the imperishable Hari cut through his bow.
And then he felled the steed that had the form of a bull. / That Daitya, trident in hand, then rushed at the lord of the universe.
Having whirled his trident, he struck the supreme lord; / but with three arrows [Hari] shattered that trident blazing like the fire of destruction.
Then the cruel, long-armed Madhu, possessing extreme illusion, / assumed the form of the Goddess, mounted on a lion, and advanced against Hari.
He struck Viṣṇu with various kinds of arrows and spoke these words: / "My husband has been felled in battle by you alone, O best of gods!
I shall slay you, along with my two sons, Skanda and Vināyaka!" / As that son of Diti was speaking, [Hari] struck him with many shafts.
He fell upon the surface of the earth, lifeless and vomiting blood. / Seeing his parents slain, the mighty one, bound by illusion,
Skanda, taking up his spear, advanced to fight Hari. / Then the Creator spoke words to Skanda, who was overwhelmed by delusion:
"Behold your parents afar, watching such a battle, / wandering in the intermediate space and standing as witnesses of the worlds."
Hearing this and then looking, he vanished right there. / Then Dhundhu and Sundhu, two excessively proud brothers,
fell upon Garuḍa in battle to bring about the death of Hari: / Dhundhu with a sword in hand, and Sundhu with a mace.
With Nandaka [Hari] cut down one, and with his mace struck down the other. / Both fallen upon the surface of the earth, those two champions were wounded and mangled.
Then Madhu quickly vanished, enveloped in darkness, / and by means of illusion cast a hundred mountains upon Viṣṇu.
Then, having cut through those mountains, [Viṣṇu] entered the midst of the darkness in battle; / out of wrath, he cut off [Madhu's] head with Sudarśana and brought him down.
Then, by the gods headed by Brahmā, by Śambhu, and by the thirty [gods], / the fame of Viṣṇu as 'Madhusūdana' was proclaimed in the worlds.

1.73.m: Vyāsa said: / Then Vṛtra, of great splendor, foremost among the Daityas in battle, / mounted upon an elephant rich as the elephants of the quarters, rushed toward the slayer of Bala.
Then, as Vṛtra was approaching, [Indra] standing on his elephant in the great conflict / pierced him in all his limbs with arrows shining like the cosmic fire of destruction.
Then Vṛtra, with a feathered arrow, suddenly pierced / the head of Jiṣṇu; by that, the mighty one was shaken.
Composing himself and raising his bow, the heroic one / showered a rain of arrows upon the body of that Daitya.
Cutting the arrows, the mighty one quickly pierced Śatakratu, / the ruler of all the gods, in battle with shafts resembling venomous serpents.
Then the king of gods pierced the Daitya with thousands of arrows; / their arrows flew at one another like the rays of the seven-horsed [sun].
Thus with thousands of arrows they pierced each other, / swift as the speed of thought, penetrating deep like mountains,
possessing the touch of the submarine fire, flying birds piercing the adamantine rims [of shields]; / the arrows of those two archers in battle were endowed with equal qualities.
Thus, in due course, the battle went on day and night. / Mahendra struck his elephant down with a pike.
Falling to the surface of the earth, [Vṛtra] swiftly went to his chariot. / Standing in the chariot, with a spear he firmly pierced that god's Airāvata,
swiftly and with dexterity, as if [striking] a great mountain with a thunderbolt. / Trembling, Indra and that great elephant both appeared magnificent.
Then Maghavan, taking up a spear and whirling it, / pierced the chest of the demon; he fell upon his chariot.
Regaining consciousness in a moment, roaring aloud, he pierced / Śakra in battle with a feathered arrow; then [Śakra] fell into a faint.
Regaining consciousness, Indra struck him with sharp shafts. / Afflicted with pain by arrows equal to a hundred million thunderbolts,
Vṛtra hurled a great trident at the lord of the immortals. / Facing the Śāmbhava weapon, the lord of gods released the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
Both weapons in the sky, resembling masses of fire, / struck one another there, emitting sparks.
At the touch of the sparks, the warriors of both armies / were unable to stand facing them, like moths in a fire.
Burned, they fell to the earth, and all fled in all directions. / The warriors of the gods and Dānavas [fled], and the battlefield became empty there.
Seeing his weapon repelled, that Daitya was stupefied with wrath. / By illusion, he hurled a weapon that was a multitude of mountains at Śakra.
With floods of arrows, Hari cut apart that mass of mountains in battle. / The Daitya unleashed the Aghora [weapon] against the mighty Puruhūta,
and thousands of crores of foremost creatures: / lions, tigers, bears, wolves, leopards, great elephants,
creatures such as serpents, rushed toward the lord of the gods. / With razor-headed arrows, crescent-headed shafts, spears, and iron arrows,
Maghavan, slayer of enemy heroes, cut them down before they reached [him]. / Then the mighty-armed Vṛtra, raising his bow, full of valor,
pierced Śatakratu with thousands of arrows resembling thunderbolts. / And cutting them with razor-headed shafts, Śakra cleaved his bow,
and instantly brought his charioteer and horses down to the earth. / Having revered a dreadful barbed mace, that best of demons
struck the head of the elephant; out of bewilderment, the tusked elephant went to the ground. / Armed with a mace, the lord of all the gods descended to the earth.
Then between the two of them a duel with maces ensued again and again. / As they struck each other, the sound arising from the blows of the maces was indeed loud.
The two executed whirls and counter-whirls again and again, / delivering very terrifying blows downward, upward, and to the sides.
Thus the battle between them became terrifying to the Lokāloka [mountain]. / Seeing it, the hosts of gods, Siddhas, and Dānavas were filled with amazement.
Those two heroes fighting came into doubt of death, / and the heroic gods and Dānavas were not at all able to look.
The lords headed by Brahmā stood in the sky to see that wonder. / By the roar of their huṃkāras and the sound of the falling maces,
the sound went higher and higher, like that produced by thunderbolts. / When the maces of both were broken, their fists were clenched.
And thus for half a watch their weapons fell. / In the meantime, the two heroes, bearing sword and shield,
advanced into the battle to fight most fiercely against each other. / Their two swords shone like lightning and meteors, and on their bodies their shields
were seen by all the worlds, who were filled with wonder at their agility. / The multicolored shields of the two were cleaved apart.
A close combat thus took place between them, / with circular movements, wheeling postures, agility, and leaping about.
The battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava was like [a battle] between Vṛtra and Vāsava. / Leaping up and quickly seizing Vṛtra by the hair,
Maghavan suddenly severed his head with his sword at the forefront of battle. / Then all around there arose a shout of victory among the gods.
With hearts full of joy, the gods honored Maghavan; / divine kettledrums sounded, and hosts of Apsarases danced.
Gandharvas sang songs, and sages chanted praises. / Terrified, all the Daityas fled in all directions, abandoning their weapons.

1.74.m: Vyāsa said: / Then the son of Tripura mounted a chariot yoked to four horses and radiant as the sun, / and spoke these words to the lord of the Gaṇas:
"Because my father was slain by your father, O lord of the Gaṇas, / therefore today I shall send you to the abode of Yama with my arrows."
Then the god, the lord of Gaṇas, said to the son of Tripura: / "In the past, by your wicked father harm to the gods
was done, a great sinful deed; was it not heard by your father? / Knowing him to be intent on sinful deeds and wicked, by the power of wisdom,"
He slew your father with a single arrow and by his might; / rescued from the mire, out of delusion he was dispatched to the abode of Yama.
"And you too, Daitya, I shall dispatch upon that very path in an instant from here!" / When [Ganeśa], the exceedingly wise lord of the troops of the gods, had thus spoken,
[the Daitya] pierced him with ten sharp [arrows] possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic dissolution. / Then, with a thousand arrows, he pierced the Daitya impetuously,
with arrows equal to Yama's rod, razor-tipped ones, and iron-tipped shafts, / adorned with heron feathers, exceedingly sharp, and having the brilliance of thunderbolt-fire.
And Lambodara, worshipped by the gods, severed his arrows; / again he pierced him swiftly with shafts resembling thunderbolts.
His whole body afflicted by arrows, he swooned and fell upon the ground. / Then Bhadra, Saubhadra, Bhīṣaṇa, and Nirjarāntaka,
each taking up his own mace, rushed against Vināyaka; / simultaneously, with strokes of their maces, they struck the lord of the troops.
Rendering their maces futile with agility, the exceedingly mighty one / then struck Bhadraka on the head with his axe;
he brought down Saubhadra's head in front with his sword, / Bhīṣaṇa's with a hatchet, and Nirjarāntaka's with a sword.
Having felled those four troop leaders, who were equal to great mountains, / Heramba then felled other hostile ones as well.
Then, having regained consciousness, the son of Tripura, best of the Asuras, / mounted his chariot and struck the best of the gods,
with shafts, crescent-tipped arrows, razor-faced ones, and broad-headed spears. / The righteous one severed them and pierced him again with arrows.
With four [arrows he felled] the horses of Sindh, and with a single arrow the charioteer; / with arrows he felled the leaders of the troops upon the earth.
Swiftly mounting another chariot, the son of Tripura / pierced the lord of the troops with shafts resembling thunderbolts.
His limbs drenched with blood, terrible in wrath and shining like Yama, / [he struck] on the forehead with three arrows and with seven between the breasts,
with four in the region of the navel and five on the fist; / with great rage, the son of Śambhu pierced the mighty one.
His whole body afflicted by arrows, that Daitya at the front of the battle / fell into a profound swoon and collapsed upon the chariot.
Then he was carried away from the field of battle by his steadfast charioteer; / the heroic Vināyaka, worshipped by the gods, did not strike one who turned away.
Regaining consciousness after a long time, he spoke words to his charioteer: / "Go, charioteer! In battle, [face] Vināyaka, the timid son of Hara!"
Then the charioteer spoke words that were true, wholesome, and gentle: / "Who is able to endure the arrows of Hara's son on the field of battle?
Therefore, O son of Prabhā, when you fell unconscious, you were brought away by me. / Knowing this now, do whatever is fitting, sir!"
Meanwhile, the best of sages, sent by the king, / revived the elephant to consciousness through the application of medicines and the like.
He caused his vital energy to be increased a hundredfold and proclaimed victory; / having first given consecrated water, he closed up the wounds on his limbs.
That elephant with his very tusks split open even a mountain; / thus, hundreds of thousands of troops and leaders of armies
the elephant, exceedingly difficult to conquer, brought down in the battle. / Sitting upon his back, that Daitya with arrows bright as the fire of dissolution,
striking them, felled the chief lords of the gods upon the earth. / By his arrows, which were equal in brilliance to the rod of Yama,
the gods, possessed of great heroism, fell, submerged in torrents of blood. / Along whatever path that Daitya went with his elephant,
everywhere he swiftly made it frightful, piled high with arrows. / Some were felled by the elephant, and others by the elephant-rider;
some gods were tormented merely by the speed of his turning. / Thus the commanders of the hosts of gods, fearless in battle, with diverse weapons and missiles
struck him and the elephant with many arrows; / nevertheless, those exceedingly mighty ones were unable to fight that elephant.
Quickly the elephant with his tusks and the son of Tripura with his arrows brought them down; / those gods whose bodies were shattered and who had not fallen to the ground,
terrified and afflicted with agony, fled to Gaṇapa as their refuge. / Seeing the slaughter of the gods, the majestic lord of the troops
struck him together with the elephant using arrows resembling thunderbolt-fire; / the elephant was arrested in his speed and surged up with an arrow.
Then the two of them pierced each other with their arrows; / both of them, roaring, desired victory over the other.
All their limbs smeared with blood, the two chiefs among heroes of the gods and Asuras [fought]. / Then the frenzied elephant pierced the mouse with his tusks;
assailed by the mouse, the elephant [fought back]; an exceedingly terrible battle ensued between the two. / Above and below, divided in parts, an extraordinary battle of the four took place,
a tumultuous, noisy battle that caused terror to all the worlds: / with tusks against tusks, and with best of arrows against arrows.
That battle became terrible in the conflict between gods and Dānavas. / The mouse pierced the exceedingly mighty great elephant;
standing at the crest of his backbone, he struck him again with an axe; / [and struck] the Daitya upon the aperture of his teeth, on the chest, and then with agility on the shoulder.
Together with the elephant, he fell upon the earth, lifeless, vomiting blood. / The sages and the gods praised [him], and said: "Well done! Well done!"
Here, others struck the Daityas in battle with unfailing missiles, / until the battle of victory between the two armies was brought to an end.
